name: MSP430F123IPWR
title: MSP430x12x 16-bit ultralow-power microcontroller, 4 KB or 8 KB flash, 256 B RAM
summary: MSP430F122 and MSP430F123 are 16-bit RISC microcontrollers with 4 KB or 8 KB of flash plus 256 B of information flash, 256 B of RAM and 22 I/O pins. They run from 1.8 V to 3.6 V at up to 8 MHz, draw 200 μA at 1 MHz and 2.2 V, and drop to 0.7 μA in standby. Peripherals are a three-channel 16-bit Timer_A, a USART for UART or SPI, an analog comparator for slope A/D conversion, a watchdog, and a flexible clock module with an internal DCO. They come in 28-pin SOIC and TSSOP and 32-pin QFN.
key_figures: 4.15 MHz at 1.8 V, 8 MHz at 3.6 V

operation.text: 16-bit RISC core with sixteen 16-bit registers. R0 is the program counter, R1 the stack pointer, R2 the status register (also constant generator CG1) and R3 constant generator CG2; R4 to R15 are general purpose. A register-to-register operation takes one CPU clock. Peripherals sit on the data, address and control buses and any instruction can reach them.

51 instructions in three formats (two-operand, one-operand, jump) with seven source addressing modes and four destination modes. Every instruction works on bytes or words. The shortest instruction cycle is 125 ns.

Besides active mode there are five low-power modes chosen in software, LPM0 to LPM4. Any interrupt wakes the part from any of them; after the handler returns the part drops back to the mode it left. LPM3 keeps only ACLK running (0.7 μA typ at 2.2 V, 25 °C); LPM4 stops every clock and the crystal oscillator and keeps RAM (0.1 μA typ). The DCO lets the CPU resume within 6 μs.

The basic clock module has three sources: the LFXT1 oscillator (32768 Hz watch crystal in LF mode, or a high-frequency crystal or resonator in XT1 mode), the internal DCO, and an external clock into XIN. It produces ACLK (from LFXT1), MCLK for the CPU, and SMCLK for peripherals. MCLK and SMCLK may run at different frequencies.

The DCO frequency is set by eight overlapping ranges (Rsel 0 to 7) and eight taps within each range (DCO 0 to 7); each range overlaps the next. Modulation bits MOD0 to MOD4 mix the selected tap with the next tap above over each 32 DCOCLK cycles to give an average in between. The stated f(DCOx0) to f(DCOx7) limits hold for every device, though each device has its own actual frequencies. The DCO settles in under 6 μs.

Setting DCOR selects an external resistor ROSC on P2.5/ROSC instead of the internal one for the DCO current source; P2.5 is then disconnected from its pad. With 100 kΩ at Rsel 4, DCO 3 the DCO runs at 1.8 MHz ±15 % at 2.2 V and 1.95 MHz ±15 % at 3 V, drifting ±0.1 %/°C typ.

LF mode takes only a watch crystal; XIN and XOUT then each present 12 pF typ. Below VCC = 2.5 V in LF mode, fit 5.1 MΩ from XOUT to VSS. XT1 mode takes a crystal or ceramic resonator, with external load capacitors on both pins valued per the crystal's specification; 4 MHz needs VCC ≥ 2.2 V and 8 MHz needs VCC ≥ 2.8 V.

Code runs from 1.8 V to 3.6 V; the highest MCLK rises from 4.15 MHz at 1.8 V to 8 MHz at 3.6 V. Writing or erasing flash needs 2.7 V to 3.6 V. RAM holds its contents down to 1.6 V with the CPU halted.

The POR releases once VCC passes VPOR (1.1 V to 1.5 V at 25 °C) and a further delay of 150 μs typ has passed, provided VCC rises at 1 V/ms or faster. To force another POR, VCC must fall to 200 mV or below at 1 V/ms or faster. A low on RST/NMI lasting at least 2 μs is taken as a reset.

Three 8-bit ports. P1 (8 pins) and P2 (6 pins, P2.0 to P2.5) can each interrupt on a selectable edge per bit; P3 (8 pins) has no interrupts. Every bit sets direction, output and function on its own. All P2 control bits exist, including P2.6 and P2.7 which have no pins; their flags can only be set by software and work as software interrupts.
A 15/16-bit watchdog timer resets the system when its interval runs out. When not needed as a watchdog it works as an interval timer that raises interrupts.

One USART with transmit and receive both double-buffered, selectable as UART or as 3-pin or 4-pin SPI. In UART mode UCLK0 is an input only. In SPI slave mode the clock on UCLK0 shifts data; in SPI master mode the part drives UCLK0. The receive input has a deglitch filter on falling edges.

A 16-bit counter with three capture/compare channels, used for capture, PWM and interval timing. It interrupts on counter overflow and from each capture/compare register. Clock sources are TACLK, ACLK, SMCLK and INCLK; CCI1B takes the comparator output and CCI2B takes ACLK internally.

Analog comparator for slope-type A/D conversion, battery supervision and watching external signals. Inputs CA0 and CA1 sit on P2.3 and P2.4; CAREF selects an internal reference of 0.25 VCC, 0.5 VCC or the diode voltage V(RefVT), and CAEX swaps the inputs. Its output passes through an optional RC filter (time constant about 2 μs) and sets CAIFG; it can drive P2.2/CAOUT and Timer_A CCI1B.

Main flash is split into 512-byte segments; information memory is two 128-byte segments, A and B. Main segments erase one at a time or all together; A and B erase singly or with the main array. The CPU can write single bytes or words in-system; JTAG and the bootstrap loader can also program. New parts may carry test bytes in information memory, so erase it before first use.
A ROM loader programs flash or RAM over a UART on P1.1 (transmit) and P2.2 (receive). Access is guarded by a user-defined password.

TEST selects test mode, which gives P1.4 to P1.7 to JTAG (TCK, TMS, TDI/TCLK, TDO/TDI). TEST has an internal pull-down of 60 kΩ typ. Keep EMI and ESD spikes off TEST; some designs need a lower external pull-down on it. Programming needs no voltage beyond the supply.

Applying 6 V to 7 V on TEST for up to 1 ms (up to 100 mA) with VCC at 2.5 V or more blows the security fuse; JTAG is then permanently bypassed. Code and RAM stay protected once the fuse is gone, provided the 256-bit loader key is also used.

On the first JTAG access after each POR, an unblown fuse is tested by a current ITF from TEST to ground: 1 mA at 3 V, 2.5 mA at 5 V. The mode starts at the first falling edge on TMS after power-up, or if TMS is low during power-up, and ends at the second rising edge of TMS; the current flows only while the mode is active and TMS is low. Holding TMS high (its default) avoids the extra current. Taking TEST low again also ends the mode.
On the RHB package, pins 4, 17, 20 and 31 are not connected inside; the exposed pad should go to VSS and be soldered for thermal and mechanical performance.
